title: Can a Team Be Too Stable
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article flips the usual retention narrative to examine the downside of too little turnover. A team that never loses anyone tends to accumulate senior, highly tenured members who strain compensation budgets, leave little room for advancement, and can become disengaged when they feel stuck. The author's proposed remedies, encouraging some senior members to move on, restructuring into more diverse subgroups, are all described as imperfect compared to preventing the imbalance in the first place. The piece ultimately argues that great teams need a deliberate mix of early-career and later-career talent, not just stability for its own sake.
points: Teams that rarely lose anyone can become top-heavy with highly tenured, highly compensated members
Top-heavy teams often have little room for advancement, leading to disengagement among senior staff
Remedies like encouraging attrition or restructuring subgroups are imperfect fixes after the fact
The better strategy is continually upgrading talent with junior colleagues before imbalance sets in
quotes: But the opposite problem can present its own unique set of problems. Some teams and organizations actually create too much stability.
A team or organization that is too heavily populated by senior and highly tenured colleagues often creates a leadership nightmare.
Not surprisingly, top-heavy teams normally have little room for advancement, so opportunities for promotion or new roles become limited.
The best path is not to allow a team to become too top-heavy in the first place.
Great teams are made up of a mix of early-career and later-career team members.
